messages.author: 5dadf4dbf792b603
messages.subject: effect size for item misfit (S_X2)
parts:
Dear all,

Thank you for the awesome package and all the informative discussions on the forum.

My Question:
Do you know how I could calculate an effect size for item misfit based on the the S_X2 statistic for a graded response model?
Due to a large sample size (N > 5000) the p-values (p.S_X2) are very often below .001 and thus not very informative (see e.g., item V10). 
     item        Zh     S_X2 df.S_X2 p.S_X2
1      V1  -63.4320 117.3874     102 0.1415
2     V10  -10.5418 193.9922     123 0.0000

Thus, I would like to calculate an effect size for the misfit.
Maybe something like the Phi coefficient = X2/n
So, maybe: S_X2/n ?
That said, the X2 statistics is based on a distribution with one degree of freedom but S_X2 statistics is based on a distribution with more than one degrees of freedom.
Any ideas?

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: effect size for item misfit (S_X2)
parts:
It is possible to convert the chi-squared variates into a standardized form, like those found in typical goodness-of-fit analyses (e.g., http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm). However, no known cut-offs have been proposed for these standardizations, so I'm not completely sure how useful they will be to you. 

That being said, you should be more interested in *why* the items are misfitting, as that's often interesting in and of itself, and will help diagnose what the problem is. I'd recommend inspecting the S_X2 tables for those items to see what is going on, and using the itemGAM() function to visually inspect an approximate the functional of the misfitting items. You may learn something interesting about them other than "they don't seem to fit". Cheers.

Phil

messages.author: 6a75f6f91a59c568
messages.subject: Re: effect size for item misfit (S_X2)
parts:
Hi,

I personally communicated with Kang, T. in my past term class who wrote S_X2 paper (Kang & Chen, 2007) in this package.

Kang says "N > 5000, I don't know S_X2 statistic will control the p-value successfully." in class. He also guessed, "May S_X2 not inappropriate when your sample size over 5000. I just test N=5000 condition in my paper."

How about consider to use the Zh statistic or S_X2/df.S_X2?

Drasgow, F., Levine, M. V., & Williams, E. A. (1985). Appropriateness measurement with polychotomous item response models and standardized indices. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 38(1), 67-86.
Drasgow, F., Levine, M. V., Tsien, S., Williams, B., & Mead, A. D. (1995). Fitting polytomous item response theory models to multiple-choice tests. Applied Psychological Measurement, 19(2), 143-166.

Seongho

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: effect size for item misfit (S_X2)
parts:
Hi Seongho,

Are you certain that's what Kang meant? That seems like a very peculiar claim to make. 

I see no theoretical reason why S-X2 would not work with larger samples (it's based on a X^2 distribution, so large samples should be fine). It probably isn't that useful with large samples, because even minute misfit will be detected, but from a theoretical standpoint I see no real issue (there has been some contention about the choice of the degrees of freedom, but for S-X2 it seems to behave correctly.....even when the item parameter estimates are known). 

In fact, in simulations I haven't seen this problem either. See attached, with different sample sizes and test lengths (using the dev versions of both mirt and SimDesign). Even with N=100,000 S-X2 gives fairly nominal Type I error rates. Cheers.

Phil

messages.author: 5dadf4dbf792b603
messages.subject: Re: effect size for item misfit (S_X2)
parts:
Thanks for the comments.
To assess the size of the misfit, I have now transformed the S-X2 into Z values
by the following formula from http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm

Z =  √(2χ2) - √(2df - 1)

and afterwards I transformed the Z values into the effect size r by the formula from Rosenthal & DiMatteo (2001)
r = Z/sqrt(N)

best,
Michael



------
Michael Paul Grosz
LEAD Graduate School & Research Network
Eberhard Karls Universität Tübingen
